partial_case.facts: The resident lived in a ground floor flat within a converted terraced house. In 2022 she reported that she could not open her windows because they had moved out of alignment. In 2023 the adjoining terraced house began extensive renovation works, which she believed caused movement in her flat. She also reported damp and mould during this period. She has since moved to a new property. On 28 February 2024, the resident complained to the landlord about subsidence caused by renovation works next door causing severe damage to her flat, with skirting boards pulling away from walls, plaster crumbling, and dust and debris falling through cracks. She reported damp and mould in her bedroom which had spread over her clothes, an unresolved leak in the basement, and windows that would not close and were out of alignment. Her flat was draughty and she kept the heating on constantly. She had reported these issues several times over the past year. The landlord issued its stage 1 response on 21 March 2024, acknowledging the issues were linked to renovation works next door and that it was trying to rehouse the resident under a major works transfer. It offered £650 compensation. The resident escalated to stage 2, and the landlord issued its stage 2 response on 3-7 May 2024, increasing compensation to £875 and acknowledging it should have monitored her flat more proactively after an August 2023 inspection.

evidence: Landlord records about window reports and repair dates.

partial_case.facts: The resident lived in a ground-floor flat within a converted terraced house; in 2022 she reported windows out of alignment, and in 2023 adjoining renovation works began which she believed caused movement in her flat. The complaint concerned the landlord’s handling of faulty windows, subsidence concerns, damp and mould, and the associated complaint. On 28 February 2024 the resident complained that renovation works next door were causing severe damage to her flat, including skirting boards pulling away, crumbling plaster, debris falling through cracks, and concerns about rodents and safety. The resident also reported damp and mould in her bedroom, an unresolved basement leak, windows that would not close and were out of alignment, draughts, constant heating use, and repeated reports over the previous year. The landlord’s stage 1 response said the reports were linked to renovation works next door, repairs could not be carried out until those works concluded, it was trying to rehouse the resident under a major works transfer, and it offered £650 compensation. The resident escalated her complaint, saying the landlord was responsible for making external walls safe, that cracks and draughts remained unresolved, and that she had sickle cell trait and was more sensitive to weather changes. The landlord’s stage 2 response said the flat was structurally safe, scaffolding had been put up to support the building, cracks and windows had not been addressed because it believed the resident would be rehoused sooner, and compensation was increased to £875. The resident asked the Ombudsman to investigate because she remained dissatisfied with the condition of her flat and wanted a direct move to another property.

determinations: Maladministration in how the landlord handled reports of faulty windows.
Severe maladministration in how the landlord handled concerns of subsidence.
Maladministration in how the landlord handled reports of damp and mould.
Maladministration in how the landlord handled the associated complaint.
orders: The landlord must apologise in writing to the resident.
The landlord must pay the resident £2,431.41 compensation.
The landlord must investigate its handling of the storage arrangements for the resident’s belongings after November 2024 under its formal complaints procedure.

key_reasoning_quotes.text: The landlord took too long to address repeated reports that the windows were not functional and causing heat loss, and it did not consider the safety or living-condition risks this created.
The landlord did not monitor the worsening subsidence, delayed essential actions after accepting the resident’s home was unfit, and failed to communicate clearly.
The landlord did not investigate the resident’s damp and mould reports or assess whether the unresolved basement problems were contributing to issues in her flat.
The landlord’s stage 1 complaint response was issued outside the timescales set out in the Housing Ombudsman’s Complaint Handling Code and did not address all points she raised.
The total award of £1,331.41 more accurately reflects the combined impact of the landlord’s failings and is necessary to put things right.
